title: POINTWISE: the thesis's founding bet, tested directly for the first time: is a judge more reliable comparing two answers than grading one? (3,689 + 3,669 graded answers; arms A with and B without the reference)
question: 3,689 answers behind R3's 1,980 matches graded once on 0-100 by the same judge with the same reference, rubric and verify-first mechanics; a pair's verdict is the higher grade; comparator the cached pairwise verdicts on exactly those matches; two-sided by registration so the thesis could lose; amended before any scored run after a 20-call probe showed grades collapsing to a 100/0 binary. Arm B repeats it with NO reference to complete the 2x2.

plain_description.what: Compares two ways of using an LLM judge on the same answers: grading each answer alone on 0-100, versus comparing two answers head to head. One arm uses a reference answer and one does not (about 7,400 graded answers).
plain_description.why: It tests the thesis's founding bet, that judges are more reliable comparing than grading. The test was set up so the thesis could lose.
plain_description.information: Pointwise winning would undercut the pairwise design. Result: done, split verdict. Comparing is better for deciding a single match (0.864 vs 0.808, significant). Grading gives a slightly better overall leaderboard (rank correlation 0.993 vs 0.979). Both effects replicate without a reference. The leaderboard advantage did not replicate on small per-area samples. Working rule: grade where answers are checkable, compare where they are not. Later ruled history rather than evidence, because it ran on the older question pool.
